page.text:
While sets are inherently unordered collections, mathematics
fundamentally requires ordered structures where the first coordinate can
be distinguished from the second—such as geometric coordinates $(x, y)$,
directed graphs, relations, and input-output pairings of functions.

In 1921, Kazimierz Kuratowski solved the problem of encoding ordered
pairs within pure set theory by defining:
$$(x, y) := \{\{x\}, \{x, y\}\}$$ This ingenious device encodes the first
coordinate $x$ by placing it in a singleton, while the pair $\{x, y\}$
bundles both coordinates together. The first coordinate can be uniquely
recovered as the sole element in the intersection of all elements of the
pair: $\bigcap (x, y) = \{x\}$.
